blocks.p: The Consistory of Life had never tried one of its own bishops, and its clerks had to go down into the archive of the first council to find out how it was done.

They found it on paper, in the minutes Aurelian had once written over: a bench of twelve, the Hierarch presiding, an Advocate to speak for the Throne, the accused to speak for himself. And one line more, which the clerks had read aloud to each other with some puzzlement, since no one could remember why it had been written: The accused shall stand bound before the bench, so that all may see he is not free.

So they bound him. It was done very kindly, in the white anteroom, by a warden who apologized for it. The chain was fine and light, of some white metal, more like jewelry than iron, and weighed almost nothing. But it was a chain, and when he lifted his hands it rang faintly, and he heard it.

The Hall of the Consistory was white and very high, and the light came down into it from a great Window above the bench, a single pane of deep living gold like the one in the cathedral at Abundance, only larger. The twelve sat beneath it in a long curve, in white, with the Hierarch at the center in a plain chair no higher than the others. The galleries were full. Sol had not expected that. Clergy in grey and white, and behind them ordinary people of Sion, smooth-faced and handsome and curious, who had come as they might have come to see some animal from the colonies. They had been told he was old. He watched the belief arrive in their faces as the wardens brought him into the little railed place in front of the bench, and the murmur went round the galleries and died.

He found Lyda at once. In the second gallery, among all those smooth faces, there was one white head, cropped short, held very straight. She did not wave. She looked down at him the way she looked at a ship coming in through weather: as if she could bring it in by looking.
The Advocate rose.

His name was Severin Tull, and Sol had known him slightly for three centuries as a fine speaker and a good host: a tall, graceful man with a beautiful voice, which he used now as a cantor uses his, filling the high white hall without ever seeming to raise it.
“Holiness. Brothers of the bench.” He bowed. “I will not keep you long, because there is nothing here that needs long keeping. I will only tell you what this man is.”

He told them, and did it well: a bishop of Life who had knelt on the floor of the Bounty Market in his shirtsleeves beside one of the infected, and taken the man’s effects into his own keeping against all procedure, and sat with him a whole night in his cell. A steward on the Concord packet who had seen the bishop seize, and heard him speak, and wept when asked to repeat the word. A Halo gone silent; of a flight by night down the back wall of the bishops’ residence at Concord, in a basket meant for the kitchen’s stores; of thirty years in the Diaspora. He laid the registries of a dozen worlds before the bench, Weir’s among them, every page, and the bench looked at them in the corners of their sight, and their faces did not change.

“Four hundred and twelve,” the Advocate said. “Four hundred and twelve souls, Holiness, whom this man has taken down into the water with his own hands, and made dark. Who can never now be renewed, nor ascended, nor received into Life. Who will wither, as he has withered, and go down into the ground.” He let it settle. “He has been a pestilence among the worlds. A troubler of every colony he has touched, from Daphne to Ephes. On Ephes, a man was killed in a riot over his teaching, and his people wept over the body in the street, in front of children. He is the head and the heart of the thing we call the dark. And he stands before you charged with the only two crimes that remain to us in the new creation: that he has spoken the name that was taken away, and that he has mourned.”
He sat. It had been very beautiful. Several people in the galleries touched their temples, as if to keep it.
“We’ll hear Bishop Croft,” the Hierarch said.
Aurelian came out from a door at the side of the bench. He walked to the witness place and stood with his hands at his sides, and Sol saw that he had not slept, and that he would not look up.
“Bishop Croft.” Tull’s voice was gentle. “You are the accused’s oldest friend.”
“Yes.”
“You corresponded with him in the Diaspora.”
“Yes.”
“Did he ever, in any letter, or on any line, or on Philippa in your presence, speak to you the name that was taken away?”
Aurelian was silent a moment.
“No,” he said.
Tull lifted his head slightly. “Never?”
“Never. Not once.” Aurelian’s voice was low and perfectly clear. “I asked him not to, and he didn’t. He told me about a man. He never told me the man’s name.”
There was a small stir along the bench. Tull smiled, as a man smiles when a good dog brings him the wrong bird.

“Bishop,” he said, almost tenderly, “the house of the Mercy Office keeps its doors. Two nights ago you were an hour in the accused’s room. I don’t ask what was said there. I ask only, for the record, whether in that hour you heard from this man the name that was taken away.”
Aurelian said nothing. The hall waited.
“Yes,” he said.
It was not loud. It did not need to be.

“I asked him for it. He had kept it from me for thirty years because I begged him to, and two nights ago I asked him to say it, and he did. And I asked him to say it again.” His hands had come together and were holding each other. “I wanted to know whether it would stay. Everything else goes, Advocate; you hear a thing and it runs out of you like water.” He drew a breath. “It stayed. I can hear it now.”
No one on the bench moved. Along the galleries two thousand smooth faces had gone very still, as people go still who have heard a door open where there is no door.
“Bishop Croft,” the Hierarch said quietly, “you need not go on.”

“I know, Holiness.” Aurelian lifted his head then, and for the first time since he had come out of the side door he looked up, not at the bench but across the little railed place to Sol, once, and Sol saw his face: not blank, not everything at once, only tired, and awake. “One thing more, since the record is keeping things. I had put my name down for a full curation at the autumn renewal. Holiness signed it yesterday. This morning, before the hall sat, I asked the east hall to strike it.” His voice did not shake. “I find I would rather keep what I have.”
Tull had not sat down. Sol watched him understand that he had been handed something he had not asked for and could not now put down. He looked to the bench.

“The Consistory hears Bishop Croft as a witness,” the Hierarch said gently, without looking at anyone. “He is not before it. Let the record have what he has said, and nothing more. Thank you, Bishop. That will do.”
Aurelian went back to his door. At the threshold he did not stop. The door closed behind him.

“Tarren.” The Hierarch leaned forward in his plain chair. His grey eyes had their dazzle in them; he had come, Sol knew, straight from the sanctum. “You may speak for yourself. Take as long as you need.”
Sol put his bound hands on the rail. The chain rang faintly on the wood.
“I’m glad it’s you hearing this, Hierarch,” he said. “Because you know the church better than any man living, and you’ll know I’m not making any of it up.”
He told them.

He told it plainly, in the voice he had once used in the cathedral, which came back to him without his calling it. He told them he had been a bishop of Life for nearly four hundred years, and that in all that time he had believed every word he preached, and signed every form he was given, and asked every time that the infected be handled gently, and believed they were. He told them about the old man in the market with the cloth bag, and the word that had been in the beginning. He told them about the cell on Serenity and the white room under the ice, and the flowers, and the needle, and the old man’s face turned up toward something that was not the ceiling.

“And then I left Serenity,” he said, “on the packet for Concord. We were barely under way when a light came over me. Brighter than the Window over your heads, brothers. Brighter than anything I’d seen in the sanctum. I fell down on the deck of the packet in front of a boy who had brought me water. And I heard a voice say my name. Sol. Sol, why do you hunt me? And I said, Who are you?” He drew a breath. The galleries had gone completely silent. “And it said, Seek Christ, and you will find me.”

He had never in his life said the name aloud to more than a roomful of people. He said it now, under the great gold Window, and it went out over the bench and up into the galleries, and he watched it go.

It went into them and could not stay. He had felt it himself, once, in a cell on Serenity, when Stephen said it to him twice and it slipped away both times like water through his fingers. Now he watched two thousand smooth faces hear it, and frown faintly, all together, as at a word in a dream, and then smooth again as it ran out of them. A woman in the first gallery put her hands over her ears, too late. At the clerk’s desk beneath the bench a young man was taking down the record with two fingers at his temple, and Sol saw him stop, and blink at the corner of his sight, and touch his temple again, and frown, like a man whose pen has skipped.

“Christ,” Sol said again, slowly, so they would have it twice. “His name is Christ. I didn’t know it. I’d never heard it, that I could remember. I went looking for it, as I was told. And I found that he’d been looking for me.”
“Holiness.” Tull was on his feet. “Let the record...”
“The record will have it,” the Hierarch said quietly. “Sit down, Advocate. He’s not finished.”

Sol went on. He told them about the three days blind, and the dockworker who came to him, and the water. He told them about Philippa and Daphne and Galatia, and the small rooms, and the copy of a copy of an old man’s notebook. “I wasn’t disobedient,” he said. “Not to what I’d seen. I went out to the colonies and told them what I’d been told: that we’d been kept, not for any good in us, and that the tears were never ours to forget, and that there was a man who would wipe them away with his own hand if we’d let him cry them first. That’s all. That’s the whole of my crime. I’m too old to have done anything else.”
“You are ill, Tarren.”
It was Tull again, and his beautiful voice was not unkind. He had come a step toward the rail, and he spoke as a friend speaks across a dinner table to a man who has had too much wine.

“Everyone in this hall can see it. Four hundred years of learning, and a sickness in the head, and between them they have unseated you. You fall down. You see lights. You hear voices on packets. Brother, it’s no shame. But you are out of your mind.”

“I’m not mad, Advocate.” Sol said it mildly. “I’m old. It’s a different thing; you’ll have to take my word for it. What I’m telling you is sober and true, and the Hierarch knows it, because none of it happened in a corner.” He turned from Tull, as if Tull had been a draft from a door, and looked up at the plain chair in the center of the bench. “Hierarch. You believe the promise. That he will wipe away every tear from their eyes. I know you believe it. I’ve watched you come out of the sanctum with it in your face.”

The Hierarch looked down at him. The dazzle in his grey eyes had changed; something had come into it, or gone out of it, and the hall had gone so still that Sol could hear the faint ring of his own chain as his hands trembled on the rail.
“Would you persuade me,” the Hierarch said at last, softly, “in so short a time?”
There was a breath of laughter along the bench, uncertain, relieved. The Hierarch did not laugh.

“Short or long,” Sol said, “I would to God that not only you, Hierarch, but everyone in this hall today, were as I am.” He lifted his hands from the rail, and the fine white chain swung between them and caught the gold light from the Window. “Except for these chains.”
And then, because it had come, and he had decided long ago that he would never again stop it when it came, he wept.

He did not do it quietly. It came up from somewhere very low, the way it had come up on the granary floor at Lowmarch and at the canteen table on Viper and every night for thirty years in the house across the yard, and he let it, standing at the rail in the Consistory of Life with his bound hands over his face. He wept for Stephen. He said his name: Stephen Hale, who had come to the market on purpose. He wept for Nell Ashby, the hydroponics technician from Concord, with her short hair, who had been very frightened and then not. He wept for Davi Coyle, nineteen, of the hydroponic decks, whose mother still had the notice with Sol’s name under her son’s. He wept for Corwin Brack and Ina Moss and Fenn. He wept for the thousands whose names he had signed in the corner of his sight without once reading them, running grey into the dark behind him, and he told the bench so, between breaths, so that it would be in the record.
“I want it written,” he said, “that I wept for them. Somebody should have. I should have, when it was my hand.”

No one in the hall moved. Along the bench the twelve sat with their faces turned a little aside, the way the warden in the white room on Serenity had turned her face to the flowers, trying with all their careful training not to see. In the galleries a few people were frowning, as at a sound they could almost place. Behind the side door, where Sol could not see him, Aurelian Croft would be standing, he knew, with his hand over his mouth.
In the second gallery Lyda did not look away. She sat very straight with her white head up and her eyes on him and her own face wet, and she let them see it.

“Let the Consistory note,” Tull said, when it was over, and his voice for the first time was not quite steady, “the second blasphemy. Committed before it.” He turned, and lifted his fine face toward the second gallery. “And not by him alone, Holiness. The woman who came here with him has wept in this hall, in front of all of us, and let us see it. I ask that she be joined to the charge.”
Every face in the galleries turned. Lyda did not move. She sat with her wet face up and looked down at the Advocate as if he had quoted her a rate she did not think much of.
“No,” the Hierarch said.
Tull turned back. “Holiness, the law...”

“The law is for those who are ours.” The Hierarch did not raise his voice. “She was never haloed. There is no pattern in her to release, and nothing in her that was ever given to us to keep. She came because he is her husband, which I’m told is a word they still use out there. She is a guest of this Consistory.” He touched his temple, and his eyes went for a moment to the corner of his sight, and Sol saw his lips move on the words of a form. “She is under my hand. Let the record have that too.”
Tull bowed, and sat.
“The Consistory notes the second blasphemy,” the Hierarch said.

The bench did not withdraw to deliberate. The twelve sat where they were and touched their temples, one after another, and spoke to one another without sound, and the gold of the great Window warmed and cooled above them as they did, like a slow breath. It took very little time. When it was done, eleven faces turned toward the plain chair in the center, and waited.
The Hierarch rose.
He stood for a moment looking down at Sol with his hands folded in front of him, and Sol saw that there was still, faintly, a line of dirt under the nails.

“Sol Tarren,” he said. “Formerly Bishop of Life. You have spoken the name that was taken away, and you have mourned, here, before this bench and before the Throne. You have said you will not turn from either. The Consistory finds the blasphemies proved.” He paused. “It is the judgment of the Consistory that you are bad hardware, and that the noise in you cannot be taken out. You will be released, gently, as is our way, and the pattern with you.”
A soft sound went through the galleries, not grief, only a settling, like the sound of a congregation sitting down.

“But first,” the Hierarch said, and his voice changed, “you will be brought before the Face of Light. You stood before him eleven times as a bishop of this church, and came out whole. You will stand before him once more. If there is anything left in you that can be healed, it will be healed there; I have never known it fail.” He looked along the bench, and no one there looked back at him. “I will take you in myself. Today. I won’t have you wait in a cell for it.”
He sat down.
They brought Sol out through the side door, into a white corridor, and Lyda was there.

Someone had let her down from the gallery; Sol thought he could guess who. She stood against the wall with her coat over her arm, and when the wardens stopped she came and took his bound hands in both of hers and held them, chain and all.
“You talked too long,” she said.
“I always did.”
“You were a bishop.” Her mouth moved. “You were very good. Even Tull thought so; I watched him.” She looked down at their hands. “Where you go, I go. I told them so.”
“They won’t let you in there.”

“Not in there,” she agreed. “As far as the first hall. I asked, and somebody said yes.” She was quiet a moment. “Then I’ll wait. I’m good at waiting. I’ve waited for ships my whole life.” She lifted his hands, and bent her white head, and kissed the place where the cuffs met his wrists. Then she let go, and reached up and straightened his collar, which did not need it, and said in the flat voice she kept for freight rates and for the things she meant most, “Don’t let it talk you into anything.” Then she stepped back, and did not say goodbye, because she had never in her life said it to anyone she meant to see again.

The Hierarch was waiting at the end of the corridor. He had changed out of the Consistory’s white into another white, plainer. He took Sol’s arm, as a son takes an old father’s arm, and the wardens fell back a pace, and they walked. Lyda came behind with two of them, as far as the first hall, where the floor changed from the white stone of the courts to a paler stone, and there the wardens stopped, and she stopped between them.

It was the long white approach. He had walked it with his heart going like a bird’s, and for thirty years he had carried it as a road made of light: the high bare halls opening one into another, each brighter than the last, until the feet seemed to walk on light, and singing came from no place in particular, in many voices and no words. It was long, and it was white. That much had been true. The light came from panels set flush in the ceiling every ten paces, and between them, if you looked, the stone was faintly grey. There was no singing. There was the breath of air handlers somewhere behind the walls, and the soft scuff of the Hierarch’s slippers, and their footsteps did not echo.
He was eighty-two, and the Earth was easy under him. The chain rang a little between his wrists at every step. Behind his left eye, gently, nothing pressed at all.
At the end of the last hall, white and tall and shut, were the doors.
He had walked toward them so many times. He had never once, he realized, looked at them. He had always been looking past them. He looked at them now. They were plain. They had no handles.

The Hierarch’s hand tightened on his arm. He looked up at Sol, his mild face shining, his grey eyes full of the dazzle, and said, very kindly, as a man says it to a child on the threshold of a room full of light:
“Don’t be afraid.”
Sol had heard it before, from a man carried past him on a stretcher in a market, with blood at the corner of his mouth.
He kept walking.
